newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian bank credit not picking up despite CRR cut-I-Sec.
newsitem.headline: Indian bank credit not picking up despite CRR cut-I-Sec.

text.p: Funds released by cuts in Indian cash reserve ratio (CRR) requirement have not had the desired effect of improving banks' slackening credit growth, ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec) said on Monday.
CRR cuts on January 4 and 18 will cumulatively augment banks' resources by 43 billion rupees, I-Sec said a report.
Over the past 15 months, CRR cuts on domestic deposits fell to 10 percent from 15 percent and that on foreign deposits has been terrminated, I-Sec said.

"Though the funds released by way of these CRR reductions have been a whopping 253.75 billion rupees, the slackening credit growth has not improved despite the prime lending rate (PLR) of banks declining by 2.0 percent over the same period."
I-Sec said the forthcoming CRR reductions will have a four-fold impact on the markets. They are:

+ The reduction in the reserve adjusted cost of deposits for banks will enable them to further reduce their PLR. Currently PLR of most banks including the State Bank of India stands at 14.5 percent, and will see a 0.5 percent drop.
Also, the spread over PLR, which is 3.75 percent now is likely to reduce further.
* Yields on 91 and 364-day treasury bills are at 8.19 percent and 10.35 percent respectively and a further drop in these is likely.

Since short-term rates have declined by about 100 basis points over the past couple of months, the Reserve Bank is likely to enforce a 0.5 percent to 1.0 percent reduction in the maximum deposit rate offered on deposits with a maturity of one year or less.

* Secondary market activity has gathered momentum and is likely to pick up further in the coming weeks. Lessons of market behaviour during the earlier CRR cuts suggest that the top gainers would be the short to medium dated securities, having residual maturity of less than five years.

Bonds likely to give the highest holding period returns over the next month would be 364-day treasury bills, 13.5 percent 1998 (conversion), 13.40 percent 1999, 13.70 percent 1999, zero percent 2000 (III) and 13.55 percent 2001.
However, the gains will not be as high as they were in the October CRR reduction since these bonds have appreciated considerably over the past few weeks.

* The Reserve Bank is likely to conduct its open market operations aggressively in January. To give an indication, the RBI had sold close to 20 billion rupees worth of gilts from its portfolio between mid-October and mid-November. The RBI has offered 13.85 percent 2000 and 13.75 percent 2005 at yields of 13.25 percent and 13.61 percent respectively.

Other securities likely to be offered for sale through open market operation windows are the 13.85 percent 2001, 13.75 percent 2001 and 14 percent 2006 since the RBI has a substantial holding in these securities.
